claims.evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing SLC6A8-HA expression pattern in Slc6a8HA knockin mice (Figure 4K).

claims.claim: High extracellular K+ stimulated Ca2+-dependent release of glutamate and GABA in brain slices.
claims.source: For example, high extracellular potassium (K+) stimulated Ca2+-dependent release of Glu, GABA, and other neurotransmitters in brain slices (Hamberger et al., 1979b; Hamberger et al., 1979a; McBride et al., 1983; Nadler et al., 1977; Keith et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and confirmed by the authors' own experiments (Figure 5).

claims.claim: K+ stimulation induced the efflux of glutamate at 0.46 nmol/min in the presence of Ca2+.
claims.source: In the presence of Ca2+, K+ stimulation induced the efflux of Glu, GABA, and Cr at 0.46, 0.33, and 0.086 nmol/min, respectively (n = 7 per group) (Figure 5B–D).
claims.evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from brain slice release experiments (Figure 5B).

claims.claim: K+ stimulation induced the efflux of GABA at 0.33 nmol/min in the presence of Ca2+.
claims.source: In the presence of Ca2+, K+ stimulation induced the efflux of Glu, GABA, and Cr at 0.46, 0.33, and 0.086 nmol/min, respectively (n = 7 per group) (Figure 5B–D).
claims.evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from brain slice release experiments (Figure 5C).

claims.claim: K+ stimulation induced the efflux of Cr at 0.086 nmol/min in the presence of Ca2+.
claims.source: In the presence of Ca2+, K+ stimulation induced the efflux of Glu, GABA, and Cr at 0.46, 0.33, and 0.086 nmol/min, respectively (n = 7 per group) (Figure 5B–D).
claims.evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from brain slice release experiments (Figure 5D).

claims.claim: In the absence of Ca2+, elevated K+ stimulated the release of a small but significant amount of glutamate with efflux rate at 0.056 nmol/min.
claims.source: In the absence of Ca2+, elevated K+ stimulated the release of a small but significant amount of Glu and GABA, with efflux rates at 0.056 nmol/min and 0.066, respectively (Figure 5E and F).
claims.evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from brain slice release experiments in Ca2+-free conditions (Figure 5E).

claims.claim: In the absence of Ca2+, elevated K+ stimulated the release of a small but significant amount of GABA with efflux rate at 0.066 nmol/min.
claims.source: In the absence of Ca2+, elevated K+ stimulated the release of a small but significant amount of Glu and GABA, with efflux rates at 0.056 nmol/min and 0.066, respectively (Figure 5E and F).
claims.evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from brain slice release experiments in Ca2+-free conditions (Figure 5F).

claims.claim: In the presence of 2.5 mM Ca2+, elevated K+ augmented the release of glutamate and GABA by 5–6 times compared to absence of Ca2+.
claims.source: In the presence of 2.5 mM Ca2+, elevated K+ further augmented the release of Glu and GABA by 5–6 times, confirming previously reported Ca2+-dependent release of neurotransmitters in response to depolarization (Hamberger et al., 1979b; McBride et al., 1983).
claims.evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from brain slice release experiments comparing Ca2+ presence and absence (Figure 5E and F).

claims.claim: Release of Cr in response to K+ stimulation was significantly reduced in Slc6a8 knockout mice compared to wild-type mice.
claims.source: While Glu and GABA were released in slices from Slc6a8 KO (Slc6a8+/Y) mice at levels not significantly different from those of WT mice (Figure 5B and C), release of Cr in response to K+ stimulation was significantly reduced in Slc6a8-/Y mice compared to Slc6a8+/Y mice (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data comparing Cr release between Slc6a8 knockout and wild-type mice (Figure 5D).

claims.claim: The basal level of Cr in Slc6a8 knockout mice was lower than that of wild-type mice.
claims.source: The basal level of Cr in Slc6a8 KO mice was lower than that of WT mice.
claims.evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from brain slice release experiments (Figure 5D).

claims.claim: K+ stimulation-induced release of Cr persisted after 10 min of washout in Slc6a8 knockout mice.
claims.source: In addition, K+ stimulation-induced release of Cr persisted to some extent even after 10 min of washout (Figure 5D), possibly due to the inability of presynaptic terminals in Slc6a8 KO mice to reuptake Cr in the synaptic cleft (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from brain slice release experiments showing persistent Cr levels after washout in Slc6a8 knockout mice (Figure 5D).

claims.claim: Ca2+-dependent release of glutamate and GABA was not affected by Slc6a8 knockout.
claims.source: Experiments with slices from brains of Slc6a8 KO (Slc6a8-/Y) mice showed that Ca2+-dependent release of either Glu or GABA was not affected by the genotype of Slc6a8 (Figure 5E and F).
claims.evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data comparing glutamate and GABA release between Slc6a8 knockout and wild-type mice (Figure 5E and F).

claims.claim: Ca2+-dependent release of Cr was abolished in Slc6a8 knockout mice.
claims.source: By contrast, Ca2+-dependent release of Cr was abolished in Slc6a8-/Y slices.
claims.evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data comparing Cr release in presence and absence of Ca2+ in Slc6a8 knockout mice (Figure 5G).

claims.claim: K+-evoked release of Cr was selectively reduced in Agat knockout mice, but not glutamate or GABA.
claims.source: Knockout of Agat (Figure 6A) selectively reduced K+ evoked release of Cr, but not those of Glu or GABA (n = 5 per group, Figure 6B–D).
claims.evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data comparing neurotransmitter release among Agat genotypes (Figure 6B-D).

claims.claim: The efflux rate of Cr in Agat knockout mice was reduced to less than 10% that in Agat+/+ mice.
claims.source: Although K+ stimulation still elicited Cr release from brain slices of Agat+/-, the efflux rate in Agat-/- mice was reduced to less than 10% that in Agat+/+ mice and 20% that in Agat+/-.
claims.evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data comparing Cr release among Agat genotypes (Figure 6B).

claims.claim: 16 out of 51 pyramidal neurons in layer 4/5 of the somatosensory cortex were inhibited by 100 μM creatine.
claims.source: Of the 51 neurons, 16 were inhibited by 100 μM creatine (Figure 7B–F).
claims.evidence: Electrophysiological recordings from pyramidal neurons in somatosensory cortex (Figure 7C).

claims.claim: Fewer spikes were evoked in Cr-responsive neurons in response to depolarizing current injections during Cr application.
claims.source: Fewer spikes were evoked in Cr-responsive neurons in response to depolarizing current injections during Cr application (25 pA step, 500 ms) (Figure 7D–F).
claims.evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing reduced spike numbers during Cr application (Figure 7D-F).

claims.claim: The inhibitory effect of Cr was reversible.
claims.source: The inhibitory effect of Cr was reversible (Figure 7D–F), typically observed within 2–3 min following Cr application (with maximal effect from 2 to 8 min) and disappeared after 10–25 min washout.
claims.evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing recovery of neuronal activity after Cr washout (Figure 7D-F).

claims.claim: The rheobase was increased during bath application of Cr in Cr-responsive neurons.
claims.source: The rheobase, defined as the minimal electrical current necessary to elicit an action potential, was increased during bath application of Cr (Figure 7H).
claims.evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing increased rheobase during Cr application (Figure 7H).

claims.claim: The number of evoked spikes was decreased dramatically during Cr application when a neuron was depolarized with a current of 50 pA above rheobase.
claims.source: When a neuron was depolarized with a current of 50 pA above rheobase, the number of evoked spikes was decreased dramatically during Cr application (Figure 7I).
claims.evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing reduced spike numbers at near-threshold currents during Cr application (Figure 7I).

claims.claim: Cr mildly inhibited the input resistance in Cr-responsive neurons.
claims.source: Cr also mildly inhibited the input resistance (Figure 7J), slightly hyperpolarized resting membrane potential (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C), or reduced amplitude of afterhyperpolarization (AHP) followed by the first evoked action potential (Figure 7—figure supplement 2G).
claims.evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing reduced input resistance during Cr application (Figure 7J).

claims.claim: 35 out of 51 pyramidal neurons were not responsive to Cr.
claims.source: The remaining 35 neurons were not responsive to Cr (Figure 7C and G, Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing no effect of Cr on a subset of neurons (Figure 7C and G).

claims.claim: Electrical properties of responsive neurons and unresponsive neurons were not significantly different.
claims.source: In addition, electrical properties of responsive neurons and unresponsive neurons were not significantly different.
claims.evidence: Electrophysiological characterization of neurons showing similar baseline properties (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claims.claim: SLC6A8-HA was enriched in crude synaptosomal fraction (P2 fraction).
claims.source: Using Slc6a8HA knockin mice and an anti-HA antibody, we found that Slc6a8-HA was present and enriched in crude synaptosomal fraction (P2 fraction in Figure 8A, enrichment score: P2/H = 1.76 ± 0.15, n = 4) and synaptosomal fraction prepared using a discontinuous Ficoll gradient (Sy and 4-Sy fractions in Figure 8A, enrichment score: Sy/H = 2.02 ± 0.14, n = 4).
claims.evidence: Western blot analysis showing SLC6A8-HA enrichment in synaptosomal fractions (Figure 8A).

claims.claim: SLC6A8-HA was enriched in synaptosomal fraction prepared using a discontinuous Ficoll gradient.
claims.source: Using Slc6a8HA knockin mice and an anti-HA antibody, we found that Slc6a8-HA was present and enriched in crude synaptosomal fraction (P2 fraction in Figure 8A, enrichment score: P2/H = 1.76 ± 0.15, n = 4) and synaptosomal fraction prepared using a discontinuous Ficoll gradient (Sy and 4-Sy fractions in Figure 8A, enrichment score: Sy/H = 2.02 ± 0.14, n = 4).
claims.evidence: Western blot analysis showing SLC6A8-HA enrichment in synaptosomal fractions (Figure 8A).

claims.claim: The sizes of synaptosomes from wild-type mice and Slc6a8 knockout mice were similar.
claims.source: The sizes of synaptosomes from WT mice and Slc6a8 knockout mice were similar, with areas of 0.245 ± 0.01 μm2 (n = 302 particles) and 0.247 ± 0.01 μm2 (n = 317 particles), respectively (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: Electron microscopy measurements of synaptosomes from both genotypes (Figure 8B).

claims.claim: Cr uptake into synaptosomes from wild-type mice was stimulated approximately sevenfold at 37°C compared to 0°C.
claims.source: Cr uptake into synaptosomes from WT mice was stimulated approximately sevenfold at 37°C (Uptake, Figure 8C) compared to 0°C (Ctrl, Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: Radioactive Cr uptake assay in synaptosomes at different temperatures (Figure 8C).

claims.claim: Cr uptake into synaptosomes from Slc6a8 knockout mice was decreased to approximately 1/3 of that of wild-type mice.
claims.source: Cr uptake into synaptosomes from Slc6a8 knockout mice was less than three times compared to its control, and was decreased to approximately 1/3 of that of WT mice (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: Radioactive Cr uptake assay comparing synaptosomes from Slc6a8 knockout and wild-type mice (Figure 8C).

claims.claim: Significantly more [13C]-Cr was taken up by SVs in the presence of ATP compared to absence of ATP.
claims.source: Significantly more [13C]-Cr were taken up by SVs in the presence of ATP, with about 10.3 pmol [13C]-Cr transported into SVs (1.03 pmol/μg α-Syp or transportation rate of 0.103 pmol/min, n = 11, Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: CE-MS and HPLC-MS data showing ATP-dependent [13C]-Cr uptake into SVs (Figure 8D).

claims.claim: Mutations in SLC6A8 were found in human patients with intellectual disability, delayed language development, epileptic seizures, and autistic-like behaviors.
claims.source: Mutations in SLC6A8 were found in human patients with intellectual disability (ID), delayed language development, epileptic seizures, and autistic-like behaviors (Salomons et al., 2001; Margherita Mancardi et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claims.claim: Creatine transporter deficiency (CTD) contributes to approximately 1–2.1% of X-linked mental retardation.
claims.source: CTD contributes to approximately 1–2.1% of X-linked mental retardation (Rosenberg et al., 2004; Newmeyer et al., 2005; Clark et al., 2006; Lion-François et al., 2006; Arias et al., 2007; Puusepp et al., 2010; Cheillan et al., 2012; van de Kamp et al., 2014; Joncquel-Chevalier Curt et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple clinical studies.

claims.claim: The estimated carrier frequency of CTD in females is 0.024%.
claims.source: While CTD is highly prevalent in ID males, it is also present in females, with an estimated carrier frequency of 0.024% (DesRoches et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a clinical study.

claims.claim: Slc6a8 knockout mice showed typical symptoms of human CTD patients with early and progressive impairment in learning and memory.
claims.source: Slc6a8 knockout mice (Skelton et al., 2011; Kurosawa et al., 2012; Baroncelli et al., 2016) showed typical symptoms of human CTD patients with early and progressive impairment in learning and memory.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mouse studies.

claims.claim: Mice with brain- and neuronal-specific knockout of Slc6a8 showed deficits in learning and memory without changes in locomotion.
claims.source: Mice with brain- and neuronal-specific knockout of Slc6a8 showed deficits in learning and memory without changes in locomotion caused by peripheral involvement of Slc6a8 (Udobi et al., 2018; Molinaro et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mouse studies.

claims.claim: Deletion of Slc6a8 from dopaminergic neurons in the brain caused hyperactivity.
claims.source: Deletion of Slc6a8 from dopaminergic neurons in the brain caused hyperactivity (Abdulla et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous mouse study.

claims.claim: Creatine deficiency syndromes (CDS) can result from defects in GAMT, AGAT, or SLC6A8.
claims.source: Cr deficiency syndromes (CDS) are inborn errors of Cr metabolism, which can result from defects in one of the three genes: guanidinoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT) (Stöckler et al., 1994), arginine-glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT) (Bianchi et al., 2000; Item et al., 2001), and SLC6A8 (Salomons et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claims.claim: All three genes causing CDS show brain disorders, indicating the functional importance of Cr in the brain.
claims.source: That they all show brain disorders indicates the functional importance of Cr in the brain (Stockler-Ipsiroglu et al., 2014; Stockler-Ipsiroglu et al., 2015; Khan et al., 2016; Fons and Campistol, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the clinical phenotypes of all three genetic defects, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Classical neurotransmitters are stored in synaptic vesicles.
claims.source: Classic neurotransmitters are stored in synaptic vesicles (SVs) (Fatt and Katz, 1950; Fatt and Katz, 1952; Del Castillo and Katz, 1954; Robertson, 1953; Palade and Palay, 1954; Palay, 1954; De Robertis and Bennett, 1954; De Robertis and Bennett, 1955; del Castillo and Katz, 1956).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple classic citations.

claims.claim: Neurotransmitters are released upon electric stimulation.
claims.source: They are released upon electric stimulation before being degraded enzymatically or taken up into the presynaptic terminal by cytoplasmic transporters and into SVs by vesicular transporters (Axelrod et al., 1959; Radian and Kanner, 1985; Radian et al., 1986; Guastella et al., 1990; Pacholczyk et al., 1991; Blakely et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Most major textbooks list either three or four criteria of a neurotransmitter.
claims.source: Most of the major textbooks list either three (Purves et al., 2001; Purves et al., 2016; Bear et al., 2016) or four (Kandel et al., 2013; Kandel et al., 2021; Siegel and Sapru, 2011) criteria of a neurotransmitter: presence in presynaptic neurons, release upon stimulation, action on postsynaptic neurons, mechanism of removal.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple neuroscience textbooks.

claims.claim: Creatine was discovered in 1832 by Michel-Eugène Chevreul.
claims.source: Cr was discovered in 1832 by Michel-Eugène Chevreul (Chevreul, 1835; Liebig, 1847) and has long been considered as an energy buffer in the muscle and the brain (Wyss and Kaddurah-Daouk, 2000; Brosnan and Brosnan, 2007; Wallimann et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is historical information supported by citations.

claims.claim: Creatine has long been considered as an energy buffer in the muscle and the brain.
claims.source: Cr was discovered in 1832 by Michel-Eugène Chevreul (Chevreul, 1835; Liebig, 1847) and has long been considered as an energy buffer in the muscle and the brain (Wyss and Kaddurah-Daouk, 2000; Brosnan and Brosnan, 2007; Wallimann et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Half of Cr in a mammalian animal is thought to come from diet and the rest from endogenous synthesis.
claims.source: Half of Cr in a mammalian animal is thought to come from diet and the rest from endogenous synthesis (Braissant et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Most of the endogenous Cr is synthesized in the kidney, the pancreas, and the liver.
claims.source: Although most of the endogenous Cr is synthesized in the kidney, the pancreas, and the liver (Wyss and Kaddurah-Daouk, 2000; Ohtsuki et al., 2002), Cr is also synthesized in the brain (Braissant et al., 2011; Braissant et al., 2001; Braissant et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Cr is also synthesized in the brain.
claims.source: Although most of the endogenous Cr is synthesized in the kidney, the pancreas, and the liver (Wyss and Kaddurah-Daouk, 2000; Ohtsuki et al., 2002), Cr is also synthesized in the brain (Braissant et al., 2011; Braissant et al., 2001; Braissant et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: SLC6 family members are secondary active transporters relying on electrochemical Na+ or H+ gradients.
claims.source: With 19 members in humans, family 6 (SLC6) are secondary active transporters relying on electrochemical Na+ or H+ gradients (Nelson, 1998; Chen et al., 2004; Höglund et al., 2005; Bröer and Gether, 2012; Iversen, 2006; Bröer, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: SLC6 is also known as the neurotransmitter transporter (NTT) family.
claims.source: SLC6 is also known as the neurotransmitter transporter (NTT) family because some members transport neurotransmitters such as GABA (by SLC6A1 or GABA transporter 1, GAT1; SLC6A13 or GAT2; SLC6A11 or GAT3) (Guastella et al., 1992; Clark et al., 1992; Borden et al., 1992; Lopez-Corcuera et al., 1992), NA (by SLC6A2 or NA transporter [NET]) (Pacholczyk et al., 1991), dopamine (by SLC6A3 or DAT) (Giros et al., 1991; Kilty et al., 1991; Shimada et al., 1991), 5-HT (by SLC6A4 or serotonin transporter [SERT]) (Blakely et al., 1991; Hoffman et al., 1991), and glycine (by SLC6A9, or GlyT1; SLC6A5 or GlyT2) (Guastella et al., 1992; Smith et al., 1992; Liu et al., 1992).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Creatine is transported by SLC6A8.
claims.source: Cr is transported by SLC6A8 (also known as CrT, CT1, or CRCT) (Mayser et al., 1992; Guimbal and Kilimann, 1993; Gonzalez and Uhl, 1994; Nash et al., 1994; Schloss et al., 1994; Sora et al., 1994; Barnwell et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: SLC6A8 is expressed in the nervous system where it is mainly in neurons.
claims.source: In addition to peripheral organs and tissues, SLC6A8 is also expressed in the nervous system where it is mainly in neurons (Braissant et al., 2001; Schloss et al., 1994; Happe and Murrin, 1995; Saltarelli et al., 1996; Mak et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: SLC6A8 protein could be found on the plasma membrane of neurons.
claims.source: SLC6A8 protein could be found on the plasma membrane of neurons (Mak et al., 2009; Speer et al., 2004; Lowe et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: 85–90% neurons in the mouse brain were glutamatergic while 10–15% were GABAergic.
claims.source: Also, 85–90% neurons in the mouse brain were glutamatergic while 10–15% were GABAergic (Meyer et al., 2011; Olbrich and Braak, 1985; Tremblay et al., 2016), which can explain our detection of Glu as approximately 10 times that of GABA (Figure 1B, C).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations, used to interpret the authors' data.

claims.claim: Cholinergic neurons represented 0.81% of total number of neurons in the mouse brain.
claims.source: Similarly, cholinergic neurons (5.67 × 105) (Li et al., 2018) represented 0.81% of total number of neurons (approximately 70 million) in the mouse brain (Herculano-Houzel et al., 2006), serotonergic neurons (approximately 26,000) for 0.037% of total neurons (Herculano-Houzel et al., 2006; Ishimura et al., 1988).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations, used to interpret the authors' data.

claims.claim: Serotonergic neurons represented 0.037% of total neurons in the mouse brain.
claims.source: Similarly, cholinergic neurons (5.67 × 105) (Li et al., 2018) represented 0.81% of total number of neurons (approximately 70 million) in the mouse brain (Herculano-Houzel et al., 2006), serotonergic neurons (approximately 26,000) for 0.037% of total neurons (Herculano-Houzel et al., 2006; Ishimura et al., 1988).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations, used to interpret the authors' data.

claims.claim: Classical neurotransmitters are stored in SVs with an acidic environment inside (pH of 5.6–6.4).
claims.source: Classical neurotransmitters are stored in SVs with an acidic environment inside (pH of 5.6–6.4) (Egashira et al., 2016; Mani and Ryan, 2009; Egashira et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: AGAT is the enzyme catalyzing the first step in Cr synthesis.
claims.source: AGAT is the enzyme catalyzing the first step in Cr synthesis (Braissant et al., 2001; Guthmiller et al., 1994) and its absence also led to Cr deficiency in the human brain and mental retardation (Bianchi et al., 2000; Item et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Absence of AGAT led to Cr deficiency in the human brain and mental retardation.
claims.source: AGAT is the enzyme catalyzing the first step in Cr synthesis (Braissant et al., 2001; Guthmiller et al., 1994) and its absence also led to Cr deficiency in the human brain and mental retardation (Bianchi et al., 2000; Item et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Medium-sized pyramidal neurons recorded had a membrane capacitance of 114.96 ± 3.92 pF.
claims.source: Medium-sized pyramidal neurons (Figure 7B) with a membrane capacitance (Cm) of 114.96 ± 3.92 pF (n = 51, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A) were recorded.
claims.evidence: Electrophysiological characterization of recorded neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).

claims.claim: There was a single previous report of Ca2+-dependent release of [3H]Cr and endogenous Cr in response to electrical stimulation.
claims.source: There was a single previous report of Ca2+-dependent release of [3H]Cr and endogenous Cr in response to electrical stimulation (Almeida et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Cr uptake from the extracellular space into the cells was reported twice previously.
claims.source: Cr uptake from the extracellular space into the cells was reported twice previously, once with brain slices showing sodium-dependent uptake of [3H]Cr (Almeida et al., 2006) and once with synaptosomes (Peral et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Knockout of the Slc6a8 gene increased excitation of cortical neurons.
claims.source: In a recent report, knockout of the Slc6a8 gene increased excitation of cortical neurons (Ghirardini et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claims.claim: Electrophysiological characterization of pyramidal neurons in the prefrontal cortex found increased evoked firing frequency in Slc6a8 knockout mice.
claims.source: Electrophysiological characterization of pyramidal neurons in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) found increased evoked firing frequency.
claims.evidence: This refers to findings from a cited study (Ghirardini et al., 2023).

claims.claim: Creatine has been reported to improve human mental performance.
claims.source: Cr has been reported to improve human mental performance (Watanabe et al., 2002; Rae et al., 2003; McMorris et al., 2006; McMorris et al., 2007; Rae and Bröer, 2015; Wallimann and Harris, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Creatine has been used as potential treatment in animal models of neurodegenerative diseases.
claims.source: Cr has been used as potential treatment in animal models of neurodegenerative diseases (Andreassen et al., 2001; Andres et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Creatine supplement has been thought to be beneficial for children, pregnant and lactating women, and old people.
claims.source: Cr is known to have effects other than an energy source, and Cr supplement has been thought to be beneficial for children, pregnant and lactating women, and old people (Wallimann et al., 2011; Brosnan and Brosnan, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: AGAT and GAMT are not expressed in the same cells as SLC6A8 in the brain.
claims.source: AGAT is also expressed in the brain, but in cells not expressing SLC6A8 (Braissant and Henry, 2008; Braissant et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Creatine and its precursor are transported between different cells in the nervous system.
claims.source: Cr and its precursor were thought to be transported between different cells in the nervous system.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the differential expression patterns of Cr synthesis enzymes and SLC6A8.

claims.claim: When SLC6A8 was completely missing, Cr treatment was not effective.
claims.source: When SLC6A8 was completely missing, such as in homozygous SLC6A8-deficient patients, Cr treatment was not effective. But if SLC6A8 was partially active, Cr was effective (Dunbar et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a clinical study.

claims.claim: Intractable epilepsy in a female with heterozygous SLC6A8 mutation was completely treated by Cr.
claims.source: Intractable epilepsy in a female with heterozygous SLC6A8 mutation was completely treated by Cr (Mercimek-Mahmutoglu et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a clinical case report.

claims.claim: The absence of SLC6A8 expression in astrocytes whose endfeet lining microcapillary endothelial cells form the blood–brain barrier indicates that Cr in the brain does not rely on import from the periphery.
claims.source: The absence of SLC6A8 expression in astrocytes whose endfeet lining microcapillary endothelial cells (MCEC) form the blood–brain barrier (BBB) indicates that Cr in the brain does not rely on import from the periphery and is instead mainly synthesized in the brain (Braissant et al., 2011; Braissant et al., 2001; Braissant, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern of SLC6A8, supported by citations.

claims.claim: SLC6A8 functions within the brain to transport Cr and its precursors not as a major contributor of Cr transport across the BBB.
claims.source: SLC6A8 functions within the brain to transport Cr and its precursors not as a major contributor of Cr transport across the BBB.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern of SLC6A8.

claims.claim: SLC6A8 mediates Cr uptake into the presynaptic terminal.
claims.source: It is thought to mediate Cr uptake into the presynaptic terminal based on studies of synaptosomes (Figure 8; Peral et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the authors' data (Figure 8) and citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: SLC6A8 is only found in plasma membrane, not on SVs.
claims.source: At this point, we do not know what is the transporter(s) on the SVs for Cr uptake. SLC6A8 is only found in plasma membrane, not on SVs, and is not a candidate for Cr uptake into SVs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the localization studies of SLC6A8.

results.result: Creatine was detected in purified synaptic vesicles (SVs) from mouse brain at intermediate levels (3.43 ± 0.40 pmol/μg anti-Syp antibody), lower than glutamate and GABA but higher than acetylcholine and 5-HT. SV purification was validated by electron microscopy showing vesicles of ~40 nm diameter, and Cr storage in SVs was dependent on H+ gradient as demonstrated by reduction with FCCP and nigericin.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C10-C14 provide quantitative CE-MS measurements of Cr and classical neurotransmitters in purified SVs with appropriate controls (IgG vs anti-Syp antibody, temperature dependence). C16 validates SV purity by EM, and C17-C19 demonstrate H+ gradient dependence using pharmacological inhibitors. The convergence of multiple independent lines of evidence (quantification, morphology, pharmacology) strongly supports Cr presence in SVs.

results.result: Genetic deletion of Slc6a8 in mice reduced SV creatine to approximately 1/3 of wild-type levels while classical neurotransmitters (glutamate, GABA, acetylcholine, 5-HT) remained unchanged. Slc6a8 knockout mice showed reduced body weight but normal brain weight.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C21 demonstrate selective reduction of Cr in SVs from Slc6a8 knockout mice (n=14) with no effect on other neurotransmitters, supported by both CE-MS and high-resolution MS data (Figure 2). The genetic specificity and appropriate controls (IgG, multiple neurotransmitters) provide strong evidence. Body/brain weight phenotypes (C22-C23) are consistent with prior literature.

results.result: Genetic deletion of Agat significantly reduced SV creatine in Agat-/- mice compared to Agat+/+ and Agat+/- mice. GABA was modestly reduced (30%) while glutamate, acetylcholine, and 5-HT were unchanged. Agat-/- mice showed reduced body weight but normal brain weight.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 demonstrate that Agat deletion selectively reduces SV Cr with quantitative data (n=10, Figure 3). The modest GABA reduction (C25) is acknowledged as less than Cr reduction (78.4%), suggesting some metabolic coupling. The genetic approach with three genotypes provides dose-response evidence. Body/brain weight phenotypes are consistent with metabolic deficiency.

results.result: SLC6A8 expression was mapped in mouse brain using Slc6a8HA knockin mice, showing high expression in olfactory bulb, piriform cortex, somatosensory cortex, ventral posterior thalamus, interpeduncular nucleus, and pontine nuclei, with moderate expression in motor cortex, medial habenular nucleus, hippocampus, and cerebellum.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C38 describe SLC6A8-HA expression patterns detected by immunohistochemistry in knockin mice (Figure 4). The use of genetic tagging provides specificity, and the expression pattern is consistent with prior reports (Mak et al., 2009; Lowe et al., 2015). However, the qualitative nature of the assessment (high vs moderate) lacks quantification.

results.result: K+ stimulation induced Ca2+-dependent release of creatine, glutamate, and GABA from brain slices. In the presence of 2.5 mM Ca2+, efflux rates were 0.086, 0.46, and 0.33 nmol/min for Cr, Glu, and GABA respectively. Ca2+ augmented Glu and GABA release by 5-6 times compared to Ca2+-free conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C45 provide quantitative measurements of neurotransmitter release with appropriate Ca2+ dependence experiments (n=7 for Ca2+ presence, n=5 for Ca2+ comparison). The Ca2+-independent component is acknowledged, and the Ca2+-dependent augmentation confirms prior literature. The methodology (brain slice superfusion, CE-MS detection) is appropriate for measuring release.

results.result: Cr release in response to K+ stimulation was significantly reduced in Slc6a8 knockout mice compared to wild-type, with lower basal Cr levels and persistent release after washout. Ca2+-dependent Cr release was abolished in Slc6a8-/Y mice, while glutamate and GABA release were unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C50 demonstrate selective impairment of Cr release in Slc6a8 knockout mice with preserved Glu/GABA release (Figure 5). The genetic specificity, Ca2+ dependence experiments, and washout kinetics provide converging evidence. The persistent Cr after washout (C48) is interpreted as impaired reuptake, which is logical but requires validation.

results.result: K+-evoked Cr release was selectively reduced in Agat knockout mice without affecting glutamate or GABA release. The efflux rate in Agat-/- mice was reduced to less than 10% of Agat+/+ mice and 20% of Agat+/- mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 demonstrate selective reduction of Cr release in Agat knockout mice (n=5 per group, Figure 6) with quantitative dose-response across three genotypes. The specificity for Cr without affecting Glu/GABA release strengthens the conclusion. The dramatic reduction (<10% of WT) is consistent with Agat's role in Cr synthesis.

results.result: Bath application of 100 μM creatine inhibited 16 of 51 pyramidal neurons in layer 4/5 of somatosensory cortex, reducing evoked spike numbers, increasing rheobase, and mildly affecting input resistance and resting membrane potential. The inhibitory effect was reversible. The remaining 35 neurons showed no response to Cr, with no significant differences in baseline electrical properties between responsive and unresponsive neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C60 provide detailed electrophysiological characterization of Cr effects on cortical neurons (n=51 total, 16 responsive). The reversibility (C55), dose-response at near-threshold currents (C56-C57), and multiple electrophysiological parameters strengthen the conclusion. However, the heterogeneity of responses (31% responsive) and lack of identified differences between responsive/unresponsive neurons (C60) indicate incomplete understanding of the mechanism.

results.result: SLC6A8-HA was enriched in synaptosomal fractions, and Cr uptake into synaptosomes was temperature-dependent (7-fold stimulation at 37°C vs 0°C) and required SLC6A8, as uptake was reduced to approximately 1/3 in Slc6a8 knockout mice. Synaptosome size was similar between wild-type and knockout mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 demonstrate SLC6A8 localization in synaptosomes by Western blot (enrichment scores provided) and functional requirement by radioactive Cr uptake assays (n=5, Figure 8C). The temperature dependence and genetic requirement provide strong evidence. EM validation of synaptosome integrity (C63) strengthens the conclusion. However, residual uptake in knockout mice (~1/3) suggests additional transporters may contribute.

results.result: Creatine was taken up into purified SVs in an ATP-dependent manner, with significantly higher [13C]-Cr uptake in the presence of ATP (10.3 pmol, 1.03 pmol/μg α-Syp, 0.103 pmol/min) compared to absence of ATP.
results.evaluation: Claims C9 and C66 demonstrate ATP-dependent Cr uptake into SVs using [13C]-Cr and CE-MS/HPLC-MS detection (n=11, Figure 8D). The use of isotope-labeled Cr and multiple detection methods strengthens the conclusion. However, the identity of the vesicular transporter remains unknown, and the uptake rate is relatively modest compared to classical neurotransmitters.

results.result: Based on relative neurotransmitter levels in SVs and known proportions of neuron types, approximately 1.3-2.15% of neurons in the mouse brain are estimated to be creatinergic.
results.evaluation: Claim C15 is an extrapolation based on the assumption that neurotransmitter content per SV is similar across neuron types. This assumption is not validated and may not hold true. The calculation relies on literature values for neuron type proportions and the authors' SV content measurements, but does not account for potential differences in SV number per neuron, release probability, or co-release of multiple transmitters. This remains speculative without direct identification of creatinergic neurons.

results.result: Prior literature establishes that mutations in SLC6A8 cause intellectual disability and other neurological symptoms in humans (CTD contributing to 1-2.1% of X-linked mental retardation), and that Slc6a8 knockout mice show learning and memory deficits. Creatine deficiency syndromes can result from defects in GAMT, AGAT, or SLC6A8, all showing brain disorders.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C74 accurately summarize established literature on SLC6A8 mutations in humans and mouse models, supported by multiple citations. These claims provide important context for the functional significance of the authors' findings but do not represent new results from this study.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on established neurotransmitter criteria, creatine biology, SLC6 transporter family, and neuronal populations in mouse brain, all supported by appropriate citations to prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C93 accurately represent established knowledge from prior literature with appropriate citations. These provide essential context but do not constitute new findings from this study.

results.result: The manuscript discusses prior work on Cr release, uptake, effects on neuronal excitability, therapeutic potential, and cellular localization of Cr synthesis enzymes and transporters, providing context for interpreting the current findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C110 accurately represent prior literature and provide important context for the discussion. C98-C99 cite recent work showing increased cortical excitability in Slc6a8 knockout mice, which is consistent with the authors' finding of Cr-mediated inhibition. C110 acknowledges that the vesicular Cr transporter remains unidentified, which is an important limitation.

results.result: Creatine was detected in synaptic vesicles at quantifiable levels relative to classical neurotransmitters. The authors report Cr at 3.43 ± 0.40 pmol/μg anti-Syp antibody, which is approximately 2% of glutamate, 19% of GABA, 266% of acetylcholine, and 3573% of 5-HT.
results.evaluation: The editor states 'The data provide solid evidence that Cr is present in synaptic vesicles.' Reviewer 2 affirms 'The study provides evidence that Cr is present in/loaded into synaptic vesicles.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'condition 1 is clearly met' (presence in presynaptic neurons and storage in vesicles). The quantitative detection data are not challenged by any reviewer.

results.result: SV creatine levels were reduced in Slc6a8 knockout mice to approximately 1/3 of wild-type levels, while classical neurotransmitters (glutamate, GABA, ACh, 5-HT) remained unaffected by the knockout.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a critical concern: 'There is no significant decrease in Cr content pulled down by anti-Syp in AGAT-/- mice when normalized to IgG controls. Hence, blocking AGAT activity/Cr synthesis does not affect Cr levels in the synaptic vesicle fraction, arguing against a Cr enrichment.' This normalization issue challenges the interpretation of reduced Cr in knockout mice, though the raw data showing reduction are not disputed.

results.result: Creatine in SVs from Agat knockout mice was significantly lower than wild-type, with GABA also showing a 30% reduction, while glutamate, acetylcholine, and 5-HT were not significantly different among genotypes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically critiques this finding: 'There is no significant decrease in Cr content pulled down by anti-Syp in AGAT-/- mice when normalized to IgG controls. Hence, blocking AGAT activity/Cr synthesis does not affect Cr levels in the synaptic vesicle fraction, arguing against a Cr enrichment.' This normalization concern undermines the claim of specific Cr reduction in Agat knockouts.

results.result: Calcium-dependent release of creatine was detected after K+ stimulation in brain slices, with release reduced in both Slc6a8 and Agat mutants. The Ca2+-dependent component of Cr release was abolished in Slc6a8 knockout mice.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states: 'There is no difference in KCl-induced Cr release between SLC6A8-/Y and SLC6A8+/Y when normalizing the data to the respective controls. Thus, the data are not consistent with the idea that depolarization-induced Cr release requires SLC6A8.' Reviewer 3 notes concerns about K+ stimulation methodology: 'High KCl stimulation is a blunt instrument that will depolarize absolutely everything in the prep all at once and could result in any number of non-specific biological reactions.' Reviewer 1 mentions the authors' response about K stimulation issues was inadequate ('No details, not data - no response really'). The Ca2+-free results are also questioned by Reviewer 3: 'why is there such a massive uptick in release, even when the extracellular saline is devoid of calcium?'

results.result: Creatine inhibited neocortical pyramidal neurons in approximately one-third of cells tested (16 out of 51), with reversible effects on spike number, rheobase, and input resistance. The remaining 35 neurons showed no response to Cr.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 challenges the interpretation: 'The rationale of grouping the excitability data into responders and non-responders is not convincing because the threshold of 10% decrease in AP rate is arbitrary. The data do therefore not support the conclusion that Cr reduces neuronal excitability.' Reviewer 1 notes the authors did not adequately address concerns about non-responding neurons. Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'Demonstration that creatine has inhibitory effects is another strength' but also notes 'Condition 4 is not discussed in detail at all' regarding receptors, and questions whether the inhibition might be 'induced by activation or potentiation of other receptors (e.g., GABAergic or glycinergic).'

results.result: SLC6A8 was necessary for creatine uptake into synaptosomes, with enrichment in synaptosomal fractions and temperature-dependent uptake that was reduced to approximately 1/3 in Slc6a8 knockout mice.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes 'For condition 6, the authors made a great effort with Slc6a8. This is a very tough criterion to understand or prove for many synapses and neurotransmitters.' The synaptosomal uptake data are not challenged by reviewers, though Reviewer 3 notes 'Regarding Slc6a8, it seems to work only as a reuptake transporter - not as a transporter into SVs. Therefore, we do not know what the transporter into the TVs is.'

results.result: Creatine was taken up into synaptic vesicles in an ATP-dependent manner, with significantly more [13C]-Cr uptake in the presence of ATP compared to its absence.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'The study provides evidence that Cr is present in/loaded into synaptic vesicles.' Reviewer 3 acknowledges the ATP-dependent uptake data without challenge. No reviewer disputes the ATP-dependence of vesicular Cr uptake.

results.result: SLC6A8 expression was mapped across multiple brain regions including olfactory bulb, piriform cortex, somatosensory cortex, ventral posterior thalamus, interpeduncular nucleus, pontine nuclei, motor cortex, medial habenular nucleus, hippocampus, and cerebellum.
results.evaluation: The anatomical distribution data are not challenged by any reviewer. Reviewer 3 notes 'Puzzlingly, Slc6a8 and AGAT are in different cells, setting up the complicated model that creatine is created in one cell type and then processed as a neurotransmitter in another. This matter will likely need to be resolved in future studies.' This acknowledges the expression pattern data while noting interpretive complexity.

results.result: The authors extrapolate that approximately 1.3–2.15% of neurons in the mouse brain are creatinergic, based on relative neurotransmitter content in SVs and known proportions of neuron types.
results.evaluation: This inference is not directly addressed by reviewers, but the underlying quantification data (C1, C10-C14) face challenges regarding normalization (Reviewer 2). The extrapolation depends on assumptions about similar neurotransmitter content per SV across neuron types, which is not validated.

results.result: Purified synaptic vesicles had an average diameter of 40.44 ± 0.26 nm, and creatine storage in SVs was dependent on H+ gradient, as demonstrated by reduction with FCCP and nigericin.
results.evaluation: These methodological characterizations are not challenged by reviewers. The H+ gradient dependence is consistent with classical neurotransmitter storage mechanisms and supports the vesicular localization of Cr.

results.result: Body weights were reduced in both Slc6a8 and Agat knockout mice compared to wild-type, while brain weights were not significantly different.
results.evaluation: These phenotypic observations are not disputed by reviewers and are consistent with previous literature as cited by the authors.

results.result: The sizes of synaptosomes from wild-type and Slc6a8 knockout mice were similar.
results.evaluation: This control measurement is not challenged by reviewers and supports the validity of comparing synaptosomal preparations between genotypes.

comparisons.comparison: Both OpenEval and peer reviewers agree that Cr is present in synaptic vesicles based on CE-MS measurements (C1, C10-C14). OpenEval finds the evidence strongly supported by multiple independent lines including quantification, morphology, and pharmacology. Peer reviewers (Editor, Reviewer 2, Reviewer 3) all affirm this conclusion without challenge.

Both address H+ gradient dependence and SV characterization (C16-C19). OpenEval integrates these as supporting evidence for Cr in SVs. Peer reviewers do not challenge these methodological validations, which are consistent with classical neurotransmitter storage mechanisms.

Major disagreement on Slc6a8 knockout data (C2, C3, C20, C21). OpenEval finds the genetic specificity provides strong evidence for selective Cr reduction. However, Reviewer 2 raises a critical normalization concern: when normalized to IgG controls, there is no significant decrease in Cr content, challenging the interpretation of Cr enrichment in SVs.

Significant disagreement on Agat knockout data (C24-C26). OpenEval finds the selective Cr reduction with dose-response evidence supports the claims. Reviewer 2 specifically challenges this: when normalized to IgG controls, there is no significant decrease in Cr in AGAT-/- mice, arguing against Cr enrichment in SVs.
Both address body/brain weight phenotypes in Slc6a8 knockouts (C22-C23). OpenEval notes consistency with prior literature. Peer reviewers do not dispute these phenotypic observations.
Both address body/brain weight phenotypes in Agat knockouts (C27-C28). OpenEval finds these consistent with metabolic deficiency. Peer reviewers do not challenge these observations.

Both address SLC6A8-HA expression patterns (C29-C38). OpenEval notes the qualitative nature lacks quantification but finds the genetic tagging provides specificity. Peer reviewers do not challenge the anatomical distribution data, though Reviewer 3 notes the complexity that Slc6a8 and AGAT are in different cells.

Major disagreement on Cr release data (C4, C40-C45). OpenEval finds the Ca2+-dependent augmentation and methodology appropriate. However, Reviewer 2 states that when normalized to controls, there is no difference in KCl-induced Cr release between genotypes. Reviewer 3 questions the high KCl methodology as a 'blunt instrument' and challenges the massive Ca2+-free release.

Disagreement on Slc6a8 knockout release data (C5, C46-C50). OpenEval finds genetic specificity and Ca2+ dependence provide converging evidence. Reviewer 2 challenges the normalization, finding no difference between genotypes when properly controlled. Reviewer 3 questions the methodology and Ca2+-free results.

Partial overlap on Agat knockout release data (C6, C51-C52). OpenEval finds the selective Cr reduction with dose-response strengthens conclusions. Peer reviewers' concerns about normalization and methodology in related experiments (R4) may extend to these claims, though not explicitly addressed.

Significant disagreement on electrophysiology data (C7, C53-C60). OpenEval acknowledges heterogeneity but finds the reversibility and dose-response support Cr effects on excitability. Reviewer 2 challenges the 10% threshold as arbitrary and states the data do not support the conclusion. Reviewer 3 questions whether inhibition might be indirect via other receptors (GABA/glycine).

Agreement on synaptosomal SLC6A8 localization and function (C8, C61-C62, C64-C65). OpenEval finds the enrichment scores and functional assays provide strong evidence. Reviewer 3 acknowledges the authors' effort on this criterion. Both note that Slc6a8 functions as reuptake transporter, not vesicular transporter.
Both address EM validation of synaptosome integrity (C63). OpenEval notes this strengthens conclusions about comparing genotypes. Peer reviewers do not challenge this control measurement.

Agreement on ATP-dependent vesicular Cr uptake (C9, C66). OpenEval finds the isotope-labeled Cr and multiple detection methods strengthen the conclusion. Reviewer 2 and Reviewer 3 acknowledge the evidence for Cr loading into SVs without challenge.

Agreement on uncertainty regarding neuron proportion extrapolation (C15). OpenEval rates this as UNCERTAIN due to unvalidated assumptions about SV content similarity across neuron types. Peer reviewers do not directly address this inference, but underlying quantification data face normalization challenges from Reviewer 2.

OpenEval R12 addresses literature context on SLC6A8 mutations (C67-C74). No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as these are background claims rather than new experimental results requiring peer assessment.

OpenEval R13 addresses established literature context (C75-C93). No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as these provide background knowledge rather than new findings requiring peer validation.

Minimal overlap on discussion points. OpenEval R14 addresses literature context (C94-C110) including acknowledgment that the vesicular transporter is unidentified (C110). Peer R6 similarly notes (C109) that Slc6a8 works only as reuptake transporter, not as SV transporter, leaving the vesicular transporter unknown.
